claims.statement: Comparing evaluator judgments to known, inspectable human examples is a calibration/alignment check; a disagreement merits examining the rubric and human label, and an aggregate agreement fraction alone neither identifies a cause nor represents all topics.
claims.scope: Calibration means preliminary checking of evaluator alignment here, not probabilistic confidence calibration or an implemented judge adjustment. The toy disagreement does not establish that a real judge mistakes fluency for correctness, and four constructed examples support no general-performance estimate.

evidence.locator: §3.3 p.5 paragraph ending “As a calibration”; §3.4 p.6 Few-shot judge; §4.1 p.7 Metrics; Appendix D.3 p.24
evidence.supports: Original research uses known identical answers as a calibration check, compares human/LLM agreement, defines the sampling target, and explicitly warns that higher consistency may not imply accuracy. Supports the methodological idea and limits, not the toy numerical score or a cause for its discrepancy.
Given literal labels and a four-position agreement calculation cannot establish a causal bias or sampled overall performance; human labels remain rubric-dependent.

claims.statement: For the same grouping-explanation task, a long useful answer and a long repetitive answer should be judged by whether the required explanation holds, rather than automatically rewarding length.
claims.scope: A normative instruction for this task-specific rubric. Original paper supports verbosity bias as a possible evaluator failure mode; this section and the CPU demonstration do not measure any real judge bias or establish that all judges prefer long answers.

evidence.locator: §3.3 p.5 “Verbosity bias” and repetitive-list attack; Appendix A Figure 5 p.13 “Do not allow the length ...”; Appendix Figure 11 p.17 explanation
evidence.supports: Primary study defines length/redundancy favoritism even when quality does not improve and supplies a rubric prompt against length influence. Its observations support the concern and task-quality principle, not a universal claim or the actual behavior of this toy label array.

evidence.locator: derivation.md manually evaluated extended equal-length examples; variants/variant-results.json exercise_manual_examples
evidence.supports: Two independently constructed 62-code-point materials show why the given rule labels useful grouping/merge explanation 1 and unrelated repetition 0; these are manual labels, not generated judge outputs.
